summary: An informational memo about producing PostScript and PDF documents that print well on both North American and international paper sizes, since these formats fix page layout exactly and the common paper sizes differ.

plainLanguage.summary: PostScript and PDF files fix the page layout when the document is created, so a document laid out for one paper size can be cut off or left short on another. This memo gives three ways to produce files that print well on both the North American Letter sheet and the A4 sheet used almost everywhere else.

subtitle: How to lay out a PostScript or PDF document so it prints well on both Letter and A4 paper.

tldr.problem: PostScript and PDF files fix the page layout when the document is created, and the common paper sizes are not the same everywhere: North America uses Letter and most of the rest of the world uses A4. A file laid out for one is often not printable on the other.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives three remedies: set margins wide enough that the smaller sheet still fits, print at 94 percent or less of full size, or buy A4 paper. It recommends PDF over PostScript for distribution.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational advice for document authors and printing software. Following it makes a document more likely to print correctly for every recipient, and the memo notes that PostScript itself has known security risks.

today: RFC 2346 is an Informational memo from May 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. Its advice still describes the same two sheet sizes and the same trade-off between margins and printed area, and nothing in the memo depends on a specific printer or on a specific version of a printing program.

sections.title: Why a Document Made on One Continent May Not Print on Another
sections.content:
Some text formats describe the exact page layout of the printed result. The memo names PostScript (MIME type application/postscript, file extension .ps) and the Portable Document Format (MIME type application/pdf, file extension .pdf) as two of them. Because the layout is fixed in the file, a document laid out for one sheet size cannot simply be re-fitted to another without something being cut off or left short.

The two common sheet sizes differ. The North American Letter format is 216 x 279 mm (8.5 x 11 in). The ISO-standardised A4 format is 210 x 297 mm (8.3 x 11.7 in). Letter is therefore 6 mm (0.2 inches) wider, and A4 is 18 mm (0.7 inches) taller. The two differences are small, but a document placed for Letter leaves too little room at the top and bottom on A4, and a document placed for A4 has room to spare at the top and bottom but is too wide for Letter.

The memo's short version of its own advice is this. If you use US Letter paper, make sure both the left and right margins are at least 21 mm (0.8 in). If you use A4 paper, make sure both the top and bottom margins are at least 33 mm (1.3 in). The memo says it is not aimed at HTML documents, though the advice may help HTML authors who use fixed-size graphics or fixed width objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDF or PostScript file says exactly where everything sits on the page, so it is tied to one sheet size. Letter and A4 differ by a few millimetres in width and height, and that is enough to push part of a page off the sheet. The memo explains the differences and then gives three ways to avoid the problem.

sections.title: Method 1: Use Wider Margins
sections.content:
The first method is to leave enough blank space around the content that both sheet sizes work. The table in the memo gives the margins to use for each combination of paper format and orientation, and the change to make when converting the document to PostScript or PDF.

For A4 in portrait, add 18 mm (0.7 inches) to the top and bottom margins, giving 20 mm (0.8 in) left and right and 33 mm (1.3 in) top and bottom. For A4 in landscape, add 18 mm (0.7 inches) to the left and right margins instead, giving 33 mm (1.3 in) on the sides and 15 mm (0.6 in) top and bottom. For Letter in portrait, add 6 mm (0.2 inches) to the right margin, giving 20 mm (0.8 in) left, 26 mm (1.0 in) right and 15 mm (0.6 in) top and bottom. For Letter in landscape, add 6 mm (0.2 inches) to the top and bottom margins, giving 15 mm (0.6 in) on the sides and 21 mm (0.8 in) top and bottom.

The memo explains why the extra room is added to the top and bottom rather than the sides: the sender does not know what printer the recipient has, and different printers feed paper in different ways, so the margin has to be there at either the top or the bottom. Left and right margins on any format should be at least 20 mm to allow for filing with ISO 838 hole punches. One practical warning: headers, footers and page numbers must also sit inside these margins, because word processors often place them outside the text margins.
sections.plainLanguage: Leave enough white space around the text that the smaller sheet still fits. The memo lists the exact margins for each paper size and orientation. The spare room goes on the top and bottom because the sender cannot know how the recipient's printer feeds the paper. Headers and page numbers have to move inside the margins too, because many word processors put them outside.

sections.title: Method 2: Print With Reduced Size
sections.content:
The second method helps the recipient of a document that already has the wrong paper size. The sender produces the PDF or PostScript file at 100 percent size, and the recipient prints it at 94 percent or less of full size, if the printing program allows it. The memo notes that many programs for printing PostScript files do not allow this. In that case the recipient can convert the PostScript document to PDF and print it with a PDF printing program, which requires the Adobe Acrobat Distiller program, which is not freeware, or a recent version of the freeware Ghostscript. The recipient may also have to specify the paper size as the size actually loaded in the printer rather than the size recorded when the file was created. It is also possible to edit the PostScript file and add a scale command before sending it to the printer.

The memo is candid that this method is harder on the recipient, who has to manage these settings. It suggests that printing software makers could make it easier, for instance with a shrink to fit paper size checkbox in the printing window and a matching default preference.

On that theme the memo recommends PDF as the preferred format for distributing documents, for several reasons. PDF printing programs typically offer a shrink to fit option, PDF has built-in per-page data compression, PDF files can be displayed without being fully downloaded, PDF is more portable, PDF renders fonts that the printer does not have in a better way, and PDF allows URLs to be embedded.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient can print the document slightly smaller than full size, at 94 percent or less, so it fits the sheet they have. That is a setting the recipient has to make, which is why the memo prefers the other methods. The memo also recommends sending PDF rather than PostScript, because PDF files are smaller, can be shown before they finish downloading, and print correctly on more machines.

sections.title: Method 3: Use A4 Paper
sections.content:
The third method removes the problem from the printing side. People in North America who often need to print international documents can buy paper in the A4 size. The memo says A4 is available in the United States from many large paper distribution companies, and that almost all laser printers support it.

Nothing in the memo requires a change to the document itself, so this is the simplest route when the volume of international printing is high enough to justify keeping a second paper size in the office.
sections.plainLanguage: Print on A4 paper instead. A4 is sold in the United States by the large paper distributors, and almost all laser printers can take it. Nothing has to change in the document, so this works well when international printing is frequent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section is short and pointed. Following the recommendations makes a document more likely to be readable and to look the same to every recipient, which reduces the risk of misunderstanding. The recommendation introduces no known new security risk of its own. The memo does warn of a different kind of mistake: relying on the recommendations might make some writers too confident that their documents will look identical everywhere.

It also notes that PostScript has well-known security risks, and refers the reader to RFC 2046 for the discussion of them. The memo's own security advice is therefore about reading and appearance rather than about the file format's behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Following the advice makes a document look the same for everyone who prints it, which reduces misunderstandings, and it adds no new risk of its own. The one real security point is that PostScript is known to be risky, and the memo points to RFC 2046 for that discussion.
